articles.title: Proofpoint Introduces Flex to Help Customers Invest with Confidence as Security Needs Evolve
articles.context: , a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, today announced Proofpoint Flex, a new investment model designed to help organizations invest with confidence by making it...
articles.full_text:
New investment model provides organizations greater flexibility to maximize long-term value from their security investments

SUNNYVALE, Calif. – October 28, 2026 – Proofpoint, Inc., a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, today announced Proofpoint Flex, a new investment model designed to help organizations invest with confidence by making it easier to adapt their security strategy as business needs evolve.

Security priorities rarely stay the same. Organizations continuously face new threats, adopt new technologies, and respond to changing business needs. Yet security investments are often made years in advance. Proofpoint Flex helps customers protect their investment by giving them greater flexibility to evolve over time.

"Customers want confidence that the investments they make today will continue to support the business tomorrow," said Blake Sallé, Chief Revenue Officer at Proofpoint. "Proofpoint Flex gives organizations more choice in how they invest across the Proofpoint platform, helping them adapt to changing priorities while maximizing the value of their investment."

With Proofpoint Flex, qualifying customers can:

Adapt over time by reallocating eligible committed spending across Proofpoint solutions at contract anniversaries.

Adopt new capabilities faster with Flex Credits that help reduce the cost of expanding protection.

Simplify technology transitions with programs designed to reduce cost and complexity.

"As organizations continue to modernize their security programs, they want investment models that provide greater agility alongside strong protection," said Mark Thornberry, Chief Business Officer at GuidePoint Security. "Proofpoint Flex gives customers more flexibility in how they plan for future security needs, helping reduce friction as priorities shift and new technologies emerge. It's an approach that aligns well with how enterprises increasingly want to manage long-term technology investments."

"Cybersecurity strategies are constantly evolving as organizations adopt AI, address new threats, and navigate changing business priorities," said Jared Crawley, Vice President of Security Sales at SHI. "Our customers are looking for partners that can help them adapt without sacrificing the value of previous investments. Proofpoint Flex reflects that reality by providing a more flexible way for organizations to evolve their security programs over time. This resonates with our customers, and we will invest in tools and resources that help them maximize the value of these agreements and realize the full potential of their Proofpoint investment."

Proofpoint Flex is part of the company's commitment to helping customers get the most value from their security investments, today and in the future. By making it easier to evolve their protection over time, organizations can respond to changing priorities without losing momentum.

Proofpoint Flex is available immediately for qualifying enterprise customers. For more information, visit www.proofpoint.com/flex.

About Proofpoint, Inc.

Proofpoint, Inc. is a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, securing how people, data, and AI agents connect across email, cloud, and collaboration tools. Proofpoint is a trusted partner to over 80 of the Fortune 100, over 14,000 large enterprises, and millions of smaller organizations in stopping threats, preventing data loss, and building resilience across people and AI workflows. Proofpoint’s collaboration, data and AI security platform helps organizations of all sizes protect their people, defend their data, and adopt AI securely and confidently. Learn more at www.proofpoint.com.

articles.title: Proofpoint Joins Microsoft Integrated Cloud Email Security (ICES) Ecosystem
articles.context: October 26, 2026 New integration embeds Proofpoint’s API-based advanced email threat detection into the Microsoft security console for stronger, defense-in-depth protection...
articles.full_text:
New integration embeds Proofpoint’s API-based advanced email threat detection into the Microsoft security console for stronger, defense-in-depth protection

SUNNYVALE, Calif., October 26, 2026 – Proofpoint Inc., a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, today announced it is joining the Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Integrated Cloud Email Security (ICES) vendor ecosystem. The new integration enables Microsoft 365 customers to layer Proofpoint’s market-leading Core Email Protection API into their existing Microsoft security environment and view Proofpoint detections directly within the Microsoft Defender portal.

This milestone builds on Proofpoint’s growing integration with Microsoft services and extends that interoperability into the ICES ecosystem to deliver a more unified security experience. Proofpoint’s integration with Microsoft’s native protection adds human-centric threat detection for more comprehensive, layered protection against email-based threats.

“Organizations rely on both Microsoft and Proofpoint to protect their most critical communications and data,” said Tom Corn, Executive Vice President and General Manager, Threat Protection Group at Proofpoint. “By extending Proofpoint’s interoperability across ICES, we’re delivering a more unified security experience that strengthens defense-in-depth and simplifies operations for our shared customers. This milestone reflects our commitment to joint customers worldwide.”

A Unified Security Experience for Microsoft Customers

Through the ICES integration, Microsoft customers can view Proofpoint’s API-based detections directly within the Microsoft Defender portal. This reduces friction for security operations center (SOC) teams by minimizing context switching and streamlining investigative workflows.

Key customer benefits include:

Integrated visibility: Security teams can see Proofpoint detections alongside Microsoft detections in a single console, accelerating investigations and improving response times.

Layered protection: Powered by advanced AI from Proofpoint Nexus, Proofpoint’s Core Email Protection API enhances Microsoft’s native controls with 99.999% detection efficacy, delivering true defense-in-depth against phishing, business email compromise, ransomware, and other sophisticated email-based attacks.

Operational efficiency: Streamlined workflows reduce analyst burden and enable faster, more coordinated threat response.

“Our focus is on building a cohesive defense fabric that drives real efficiency for security operations centers, anchored in Microsoft Defender,” said Oz Wilder, Partner Director for email and collaboration security, Microsoft. “The ICES ecosystem enables customers to adapt and scale with the evolving threat landscape. By integrating with Microsoft Defender, Proofpoint helps deliver a more consistent and simplified security operations experience for shared customers in Microsoft Defender.”

Partnership Momentum Accelerates

Proofpoint protects more than 1.8 million Microsoft customers worldwide, making its participation in ICES a natural evolution of the partnership and a commitment to delivering tightly integrated security experiences.

With industry-leading, human-centric threat detection and a proven record of protecting enterprise email at scale, Proofpoint brings depth and interoperability to the Microsoft security ecosystem.

For more information, please visit https://www.proofpoint.com/us/api-email-security or read our blog at https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-protection/proofpoint-joins-microsoft-defender-ices-vendor-ecosystem.

articles.title: Proofpoint CEO Sumit Dhawan On ‘Market-Changing’ $6.3B Varonis Deal, IPO Goal
articles.context: 3 billion deal for publicly traded Varonis was announced—Dhawan said that the planned acquisition seeks to bring together complementary technologies for securing data and AI...
articles.full_text:
The planned acquisition of publicly traded data security vendor Varonis will enable Proofpoint partners to deliver a ‘comprehensive data security solution to their customers,’ which is primed for combating AI and agentic risk, Dhawan tells CRN.

Amid the surging adoption of AI agents, Proofpoint’s “market-changing” deal to acquire Varonis is aimed squarely at helping partners and customers to protect the data those agents can access, Proofpoint CEO Sumit Dhawan told CRN.

In an interview Friday—a day after Proofpoint’s $6.3 billion deal for publicly traded Varonis was announced—Dhawan said that the planned acquisition seeks to bring together complementary technologies for securing data and AI agents, while giving partners an even more strategic role with their customers.

[Related: 5 Things To Know On Proofpoint’s $6.3B Acquisition Of Varonis]

The deal ultimately is positioned to enable Proofpoint partners to deliver customers a broader data security platform that is primed for combating AI and agentic risk, he said.

With the combined Proofpoint-Varonis platform that is envisioned, partners will be enabled to “take a comprehensive data security solution to their customers—becoming more strategic, providing more value-added services,” Dhawan said. “And No. 2, they now can work with a single [data security] provider with a larger business.”

The combination of Varonis with Proofpoint, which was itself publicly traded until its acquisition by private equity firm Thoma Bravo in 2021, is also poised to strengthen Proofpoint’s positioning for an initial public offering, Dhawan told CRN.

“We think it’s going to be even more attractive to public investors, and our goal would be to assess that after close,” he said.

The combined company would have more than 8,000 employees with annual recurring revenue (ARR) of more than $3 billion, according to figures disclosed by the companies.

Upon completion of the combination of the two vendors, “it’s a top-five cybersecurity company with healthy growth—and more importantly, [providing] the next frontier of protection, which is data,” Dhawan said.

What follows is more of CRN’s interview with Dhawan.

What does this deal mean for the industry and the channel?

It’s a game-changing moment—just bringing together Varonis and Proofpoint makes us the [premier] data security solution in the market, especially in the world of AI. So we’re very excited.

It sounds like the ultimate plan is for this to be a combined solution from the two companies, as opposed to being Varonis operating independently of Proofpoint?

[Varonis CEO] Yaki [Faitelson] and I started the conversations a while ago. And we always compare notes on the market and whatnot. [We are] largely complementary. And earlier this year, as this whole agentic era starts shaping up, we said, look, there is clearly a next frontier on cybersecurity emerging, which is data. AI is attacking data from outside, and AI is attacking data [from] inside. And data protection needs to be done holistically. That was the vision that brought us together—to say, not just that we can have one house that will be able to serve all the portfolio. But if you’re really providing data protection, it needs to be done with machine speed. And machine-speed level of protection, in the world of AI, means integrations of our signals and control points. And that’s what our vision is. We believe we can accomplish that very, very quickly, based on just how complementary our technology stack is.

What are you hearing from your customers and your partners about how urgent of a need there is for something like this?

The whole conviction of ours is rooted on the principle that this is a board- and CEO-level priority. [When] you think about it, AI and cybersecurity, those are the two priorities for the board and CEOs. And they go hand-in-hand. Without data security, you can’t enable and adopt AI. So to me, that sort of is the grounding fact for the conviction that we have, on why data becomes the next frontier for cybersecurity—and why Proofpoint and Varonis becomes the only player that no other [vendor] can do, [providing] a full and comprehensive solution for protecting data in today’s AI-accelerated risks.

Can you say whether the combined company will operate entirely under the Proofpoint brand, or whether Varonis will still exist as a brand in some form?

We’re going to talk through it—we’re going to think that through. Those things get sorted out as we go. [Both companies have a] strong product, strong following in the customer base. So we don’t have any desired intent to make one change or the other. But it’s something we’ll figure out between now and close [of the deal].

As far as what Varonis brings in product capabilities, what specifically are you most excited about? And what do you think partners are going to be really excited about from Varonis?

What Proofpoint has built is sensing how people and AI behave when they’re interacting with data and each other—that’s our focus area. Intent-based protection, as we’ve always talked about, when people, AI and data come together. What Varonis has built is making sure that [businesses understand] where the data is and how it is getting protected based on privileges and usage. So these are a complementary set of signals. We are getting the signals on the intent and behavior, and they’re getting the signals at the data layer. Combining the two together gives you the right protection of data in today’s AI and machine-speed era. That’s the complementary nature of the solution. I’ve gotten so many positive feedback in less than 24 hours, and it’s all been about this—[they’ve been] waiting for [a vendor] who brings data security together. And Proofpoint and Varonis, because of the complementary nature of the solution, [can] become that company.

It sounds like some of the capabilities that Varonis has in certain areas are bringing something a bit different to your platform?

We already have data security solutions. We’re the market leader for DLP [data loss prevention]. We’re the market leader for insider risk solution. Those are complementary to the data security and access governance solution that Varonis brings. You combine them together, and now you can protect data at rest, and you can protect data in motion, as used by humans and AI. So think of it as data security at two different layers, working together, through a combination of signals and protection.

Are you saying how many employees the combined company will have?

Varonis has more than 2,500 employees [and] publicly we have said we have closer to 5,500 employees. As a combined company, it’s an at-scale company. We have publicly said that our ARR exiting midyear was closer to $2.5 billion. They have publicly said a little shy of $800 million exiting June. So you’re talking about a company of scale. It’s a top-five cybersecurity company with healthy growth—and more importantly, [providing] the next frontier of protection, which is data.

Envisioning the bringing together and combining of these two companies, you would say this is going to be very differentiated?

If you look at other top-five cybersecurity companies, none of those platforms were designed and built to do data protection. They’re [from] different eras of cybersecurity—endpoint, network. We become, together, the company that protects data from external threats as well as insiders. Both are being accelerated because of AI.

On the partner front, what should partners of both companies know about what this means?

Partners are excited. It happened to be that yesterday we had a European partner council, and our head of Europe was running that partner council when the news broke. And many of them said, “Hey, look, Varonis is one of our top partners. Proofpoint is one of our top partners. Together, you become maybe the No. 1 or No. 2 partner of ours going forward.” From a partner’s perspective, No. 1, most importantly, they can take a comprehensive data security solution to their customers—becoming more strategic, providing more value-added services. And No. 2, they now can work with a single provider with a larger business—which is what partners want, anyway.

Previously you talked about potentially going public at some point—probably it’s not something you would be looking at doing prior to closing this, but is there any update there?

Like you said, our focus is going to be on [closing the acquisition]. And we hope to go through the regulatory process and close the transaction as early as possible. And then we think that the combined company is quite attractive to the public investors. It’s an at-scale company, driving protection of one of the key pillars, just like any other major cybersecurity platforms are doing. We think it’s going to be even more attractive to public investors. And our goal would be to assess that after close.

Agents are something that so many businesses are grappling with, and it sounds like this combination is very much going to be tuned toward helping companies with that?

Exactly. There isn’t a day that goes by whereby we don’t read the news about risks that AI agents pose. Risks that AI agents pose doesn’t mean you have to slow down the adoption. It just means that you need to adopt AI with the right degree of security. What are these risks going after? You read all these stories. Eventually, the issue is that these AI agents go to data [systems], and the data is captured in so many different places. So enterprises need comprehensive solution that can both work on protecting the behavior of AI and protecting the data, regardless of where it exists. And that’s what Proofpoint and Varonis offers. It provides a solution that enables enterprises to go pick any agents of their choice. They’re not locked in. Go pick and enable access to any data of their choice. And in that environment, their data is protected, and they can adopt AI with speed.

There are so many different vendors coming out and saying they’re going to have some solution to this. But it sounds like part of the idea here is if you’re already protecting the data—as you and Varonis are—then you’re really in the best position to help with the agent problem, if the agent is ultimately trying to access data?

That’s 100-percent right. There is no use solving a sliver of the problem. These are interconnected problems—because eventually, agents have to access data. By protecting data, you extend that protection to protecting AI agents. So that’s why our solution in protecting agentic security—through an extension of protecting data—becomes even more powerful and real for customers.

Overall, what is the message for your partners out of this, and what is the major opportunity for them?

Firstly, I want to thank the partners that have really built the business for us. We couldn’t do it without them. And this is game-changing. It’s a market-changing, game-changing [deal], really helping customers together with partners. We can be their strategic advisors, a platform for protecting the next frontier of cybersecurity, which is data, and all driven because of AI.

articles.title: Proofpoint to Acquire Varonis in a $6.3 Billion Transaction
articles.context: (“Proofpoint”), a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, today announced entrance into a definitive agreement under which Varonis will be acquired by Proofpoint, a...
articles.full_text:
Combination creates a new cybersecurity powerhouse to deliver a complete security platform that protects against AI-accelerated threats and data risks

MIAMI, FL and SUNNYVALE, CA – October 15, 2026 – Varonis Systems, Inc. (Nasdaq: VRNS) (“Varonis”), the data and AI security leader, and Proofpoint, Inc. (“Proofpoint”), a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, today announced entrance into a definitive agreement under which Varonis will be acquired by Proofpoint, a portfolio company of Thoma Bravo, in an all-cash transaction valued at approximately $6.3 billion.

Under the terms of the agreement, Varonis shareholders will receive $49.75 per share in cash. This purchase price represents a premium of 52% to Varonis’ closing stock price of $32.71 on June 22, 2026, the last full trading day prior to initial rumors about a potential sale of the Company, and a premium of 17% over Varonis’ closing stock price of $42.35 on September 1, 2026, the last trading day prior to additional media reports speculating about a potential sale of Varonis. The transaction values Varonis at approximately 53x LTM Free Cash Flow and 8.4x LTM Revenue.1

The combined company will serve more than 16,000 enterprises and millions of organizations globally, creating one of the world’s leading pure-play cybersecurity companies and establishing the industry's largest data and AI cybersecurity organization. Together, the combined company intends to deliver a unified platform that helps organizations adopt AI with confidence: finding and protecting sensitive data, controlling what people and AI can access, and stopping data loss. Following closing, Proofpoint intends to move quickly to integrate the companies’ capabilities, align go-to-market efforts, and accelerate delivery of the combined platform to customers.

“Today begins an exciting new chapter for Varonis and our customers. It’s a testament to the incredible work of the Varonis team over two decades,” said Yaki Faitelson, Varonis CEO, Co-Founder and Chairman of the Board of Directors. “Our mission is to secure AI and the data that powers it. By joining forces with Proofpoint, we can achieve this mission faster than ever.”

Faitelson continued, “This announcement follows a comprehensive evaluation led by a committee of independent members of our Board of Directors, which included extensive outreach to a range of potential strategic and financial buyers. This transaction is an excellent outcome for the company and our shareholders, representing a realization of immediate, significant, and certain value well in excess of the risk-adjusted value of delivering against our standalone plan.”

“As AI becomes embedded across the enterprise, the data it can access determines both its value and its risk. AI agents are increasingly accessing sensitive information and taking action across systems, making it critical for organizations to understand not only what data needs protecting and who can access it, but how it is actually being used,” said Sumit Dhawan, CEO of Proofpoint. “By connecting communications, identities, permissions, data, and AI, we are creating an intelligence advantage that helps customers see risk more clearly, respond faster, and defend against the next generation of AI risks. This is a defining step in Proofpoint’s evolution into a cybersecurity platform built for the future of AI.”

Transaction Details

The transaction, which has been unanimously approved by the Varonis Board of Directors, is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to customary closing conditions, including approval by Varonis shareholders and receipt of regulatory approvals. Thoma Bravo is providing committed equity financing, and has secured debt financing commitments, to fund the purchase. Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan has also agreed to make an investment into Proofpoint in connection with the transaction. Until the transaction closes, Proofpoint and Varonis will continue to operate as separate and independent companies. Upon completion of the transaction, Varonis' common stock will cease trading on the Nasdaq, and Varonis will become a private company.

Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results

Varonis will announce its financial results for the third quarter 2026 following the close of the U.S. financial markets on November 3. The news release will be available on the Investor Relations section of the company’s website. In light of the announced transaction, Varonis will not conduct an earnings conference call.

Advisors

Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC is acting as exclusive financial advisor and Paul Hastings LLP is serving as legal counsel to Varonis.

BofA Securities, Inc., Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC, J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, UBS Securities LLC, and Mizuho Securities USA LLC are serving as financial advisors, and Kirkland & Ellis LLP is serving as legal counsel to Proofpoint.

About Varonis

Varonis (Nasdaq: VRNS) secures AI and the data that powers it. The Varonis platform gives organizations automated visibility and control over their critical data wherever it lives and helps ensure safe and trustworthy AI from code to runtime. Backed by 24x7x365 managed detection and response, Varonis gives thousands of organizations worldwide the confidence to adopt AI, reduce data exposure, and stop AI-powered threats.

Proofpoint, Inc. is a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, securing how people, data and AI agents connect across email, cloud and collaboration tools. Proofpoint is a trusted partner to over 80 of the Fortune 100, over 14,000 large enterprises, and millions of smaller organizations in stopping threats, preventing data loss, and building resilience across people and AI workflows. Proofpoint’s collaboration, data, and AI security platform helps organizations of all sizes protect their people, defend their data, and adopt AI securely and confidently. articles.title: Healthcare Sees No Relief from Cyberattacks Disrupting Patient Care

articles.full_text:
New Proofpoint-Ponemon Institute report finds nearly three in four U.S. healthcare organizations experienced disruption to patient care due to cyberattacks

SUNNYVALE, Calif.– October 13, 2026 – Proofpoint, Inc., a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, and Ponemon Institute, a top IT security research organization, today released findings from their fifth annual Cyber Insecurity in Healthcare report, revealing that cyberattacks are increasing in frequency, cost, and operational impact across U.S. healthcare organizations.

97% of organizations surveyed experienced at least one cyberattack in the past 12 months, of which 74% reported disruption to patient care as a result. The average number of attacks climbed to 51, from 43 in 2025, and the average cost of the most expensive cyberattack rose nearly 8% to $4.2 million. AI adoption is also outpacing governance, with AI agents operating without guardrails emerging as a leading cause of data loss, cited by 24% of respondents.

“Cyber resilience has become essential to healthcare resilience,” said Ryan Kalember, chief strategy officer, Proofpoint. “When a cyberattack delays a procedure, extends a hospital stay, or forces patients to another facility, cyber risk becomes patient risk. AI is now adding another dimension as people and AI systems access the same sensitive data and clinical workflows. Healthcare organizations need security built around those interactions so they can adopt AI without compromising the trust patient care depends on.”

This year’s report, based on responses from 705 IT and IT security practitioners at U.S. healthcare organizations, highlights several trends:

Operational disruption is becoming healthcare’s biggest cyber cost

More attacks are driving higher costs and greater disruption. The average cost of the most expensive cyberattack increased from $3.9 million in 2025 to $4.2 million in 2026.

Downtime and recovery carry the greatest financial impact. Disruption to normal healthcare operations averaged $1.39 million—the single largest cost category—followed by $1.05 million from idle time and lost productivity.

AI adoption is moving faster than governance

AI is becoming part of healthcare operations and security. 45% of organizations have embedded AI in cybersecurity or both cybersecurity and patient care, while another 30% plan to adopt it.

Security and governance have not kept pace. 60% lack controls governing sensitive data used in AI systems, only 42% use security measures specifically designed for AI systems, agents and generative AI, and just 32% have full visibility into employees’ use of unsanctioned AI tools.

AI is introducing new dependencies and data risks. Supply chain risk from AI vendors (40%), data leakage through prompts (36%) and AI-generated phishing and social engineering (34%) are organizations’ leading AI-specific concerns.

Cyber disruption is reaching the bedside

Cyberattacks are directly affecting patient care. Across the four attack types studied—cloud/account compromise, ransomware, supply chain attacks, and business email compromise (BEC) —an average of 53% of respondents reporting care disruption cited increased complications from medical procedures, 52% cited longer patient stays, and 52% cited delays in tests or procedures.

Supply chain attacks had the greatest impact on patient care. 90% of organizations experiencing these attacks reported care disruption, up from 87% in 2025. Ransomware was most associated with longer patient stays (70%), while BEC was most associated with delays in procedures and tests resulting in poor outcomes (68%).

Data loss is also a patient-care risk. Organizations experienced an average of 21 data loss or exfiltration incidents involving sensitive healthcare information over two years. 54% said these incidents disrupted patient care; among that group, 56% reported increased mortality rates. Employee negligence remained the leading reported cause of data loss, while AI agents without guardrails emerged as a cause for 24%.

Healthcare’s move to the cloud is raising the stakes of account compromise. 35% of organizations have moved clinical applications to the cloud, up from 30% in 2025, while another 44% plan to do so within the next two years. Yet cloud/account compromises — up to 20 per organization on average — disrupted patient care for 65% of respondents, a number climbing as adoption accelerates.

Ransomware payments decline, but disruption persists

Fewer organizations are paying ransoms, and payments are falling. 31% of organizations experiencing ransomware paid, down from 33% in 2025, while the average costliest ransom payment fell from $1.2 million to $1.1 million.

The clinical consequences remain significant. 72% of organizations experiencing ransomware reported patient-care disruption, up from 67% in 2025. Among those reporting disruption, 70% cited longer patient stays.

To download the 2026 Study on Cyber Insecurity in Healthcare: The Cost and Impact on Patient Safety and Care, please visit: https://www.proofpoint.com/us/resources/threat-reports/ponemon-healthcare-cybersecurity-report

To read our blog, please visit: https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/thought-leadership/cyber-insecurity-healthcare-2026-ai-adoption-accelerating-governance-needs

Healthcare Cyberattacks Hit Harder, Cost More

Study Warns of Rising Attacks, Care Disruptions, Added Costs and New AI Risks Marianne Kolbasuk McGee (HealthInfoSec) • October 13, 2026

Credit Eligible

The frequency of cyberattacks on healthcare organizations, the disruption of those incidents on patient care, workflow and hospital operations - and their associated financial costs - are climbing, according to new research.

See Also: Live Webinar | Hurtling Toward a Cybersecurity Crisis: The Hidden AI Risks Businesses Can’t See

A survey of 705 IT and IT security practitioners at U.S. healthcare institutions conducted in May 2026 found that nearly all organizations had experienced at least one cyberattack within the last year, according to the new report by the research firm Ponemon Institute and security vendor Proofpoint released on Tuesday.

Operational disruption expenses related to the attacks now account for the single-largest cost of a cyberattack, averaging $1.39 million, the research found. That's up from $1.2 million in 2025, which includes expenses stemming from system unavailability.

"When critical systems go down, the consequences extend well beyond financial losses to delayed procedures, longer hospital stays and interruptions in essential patient services," said Susan Biddle, director of healthcare solutions at Proofpoint.

We're seeing more attacks, higher costs and greater disruption to patient care," she told ISMG.

In fact, 97% of survey respondents said their organizations experienced at least one cyberattack in the past 12 months, of which 74% reported disruption to patient care as a result. The average number of attacks organizations reported also rose - to 51, from 43 in 2025.

The average cost of the most expensive cyberattack also rose nearly 8% to $4.2 million, up from $3.9 million in 2025.

"What concerns me most is that cyberattacks are increasingly becoming healthcare operational crises, not just IT incidents," Biddle said.

But when it comes to the costs associated with the attacks, fewer healthcare organizations are paying extortion demands even as ransomware continues to disrupt patient care. "It's a reminder that avoiding a ransom payment doesn't necessarily mean avoiding the consequences of an attack," she said.

"Ultimately, the findings point to a broader shift in how we think about healthcare cybersecurity. Success can't be measured only by the attacks stopped or data protected. It also has to be measured by whether clinicians can continue doing their jobs and patients can continue receiving care."

At the same time, healthcare providers are embracing AI faster than they can secure and govern it, she said. The survey found that 45% of organizations have embedded AI in cybersecurity - or in both cybersecurity and patient care - while another 30% plan to adopt it.

Sixty percent of the respondents admitted their organizations lacked controls governing sensitive data used in AI systems, with only 42% saying they use security measures designed for AI.

Those Ponemon Institute/Proofpoint findings appear to sync with other recent findings by other researchers. For instance, recent research by privacy and security consulting firm Clearwater found similar gaps between AI adoption in healthcare and the lack of governance (see: Healthcare AI Governance Has Visibility Problem).

AI technologies hold enormous promise for improving care and efficiency, but many organizations still lack the visibility and governance needed to manage the risks, Biddle said. "That gap is particularly concerning in an industry where sensitive data and operational continuity are so closely tied to patient outcomes."

The AI-specific risk of greatest concern according to nearly 40% of the survey respondents was supply chain risk from AI vendors. That was followed by other AI risk concerns, including data leakage via prompts; AI-generated phishing and social engineering scams; inadequate privacy protections; and non-compliant tool usage.

"Healthcare organizations don't necessarily need to slow AI adoption, but security needs to evolve alongside it rather than follow it," Biddle told ISMG. That starts with understanding where AI is being used, what sensitive information it can access and what actions AI agents are permitted to take.

"Our research found that 60% of organizations lack controls governing sensitive data used in AI systems. That's a gap healthcare leaders need to prioritize as AI becomes more embedded in clinical and operational workflows."

But healthcare organizations can't neglect human risks that have long made the sector vulnerable, from phishing and compromised accounts to employee mistakes and data loss, she said. "As people and AI agents increasingly work alongside one another, the priority should be protecting those interactions while ensuring critical healthcare services remain available."

Resiliency in the face of disruptive healthcare cyberattacks was also top of mind of many experts who spoke at the ISMG HealthSec cybersecurity summit in New York City last week.

"Moving from cyber defense to cyber resilience is important for anybody in any sector, but I would argue that it's even more important for the healthcare sector," said Guru Gurushankar, senior vice president and general manager of healthcare and life sciences at security firm Color Tokens.

"In healthcare, I cannot turn away patients during the downtime. I cannot turn away ambulances. I cannot reschedule elective surgeries and even emergent surgeries," he said. Cyber resilience plays a critical role in delivering uninterrupted clinical care, he said. That requires certain key technical controls.

"Microsegmentation has to be core essential because that is the proactive way in which you prevent a simple breach incident from becoming a large-scale catastrophic incident," he said.

Proofpoint's Biddle said she expects the line between cybersecurity and healthcare resilience to become increasingly blurred.

"As clinical applications move to the cloud and AI becomes more embedded in everyday workflows, healthcare organizations will face growing pressure to secure not just their systems and data, but the processes that keep patient care moving," she said.

The question will increasingly shift from whether an organization can prevent every attack to how effectively it can maintain and restore critical services when something goes wrong, she added.

"AI will add another dimension to that challenge. As agents take on more responsibility, healthcare organizations will need to move beyond governing who can access sensitive information to understanding what AI systems can do with it," she said.

AI governance, data protection and third-party risk will ultimately become much more central to healthcare cybersecurity strategies moving forward, she predicted.

articles.title: The Hidden AI Security Risks Threatening Businesses
articles.context: Externally, AI accelerates vulnerability exploitation, making faster patching and continuous monitoring critical
articles.full_text:
getty

As businesses race to adopt artificial intelligence, new security risks are emerging alongside the technology’s benefits. These threats are challenging traditional security practices and introducing vulnerabilities that organizations may not be equipped to recognize or manage. As AI takes on a greater role in daily workflows and decision-making, leaders must understand how their organizations’ exposure is changing.

Protecting business systems and sensitive information requires more than adapting existing cybersecurity defenses; it also means considering the unique risks associated with AI technologies. Below, members of Forbes Technology Council highlight AI security risks business and tech leaders need to understand and share practical ways organizations can address them.

Sensitive Data Exposure Through AI Prompts

AI prompts can silently leak more sensitive information than most tech leaders imagine. For any AI tool, understand what goes into the underlying LLM, who hosts it and what privacy and security measures are provided. The more concentrated your LLM infrastructure or provider, the better your chance to guardrail your business’s sensitive information. - Alekh Jindal, Tursio

AI-Accelerated Zero-Day Exploits

AI makes it very easy to find and exploit zero-day vulnerabilities in an operating system, hypervisor or anywhere in infrastructure. This means that the whack-a-mole game of patching systems as quickly as possible won’t work anymore. What tech leaders need to understand is that the game has shifted to prevention—the key is securing the infrastructure in a way that, even if there’s a zero-day, the data is still safe. - Ayal Yogev, Anjuna Security

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Unchecked AI Agent Authority

The AI security risk leaders should watch is unchecked AI authority. Internally, as AI agents move from recommending to executing, organizations need clear permissions, policy-based authorization, approval thresholds and audit trails. Externally, AI accelerates vulnerability exploitation, making faster patching and continuous monitoring critical. The goal is not to restrict AI autonomy but to ensure it is governed at the point of action. - Shahir Daya, Zafin

Third-Party AI Data Exposure

Sending data, especially PII data and legal and compliance-sensitive data, through a direct API or MCP connection to a third-party model like OpenAI or Anthropic creates a new trust boundary. That data now flows through infrastructure you don’t control. Self-hosted models keep data and inference in one environment, reducing third-party exposure and the number of trust boundaries that can fail. - Julia Penfield, PH.D., VelocityEHS

Unmonitored AI Tools With Data Access

Ask security how many AI tools and agents employees connected to company data last month—most can’t answer, and that blind spot is the real exposure, not the AI itself. Treat every AI tool like a company laptop: Give it an owner, log what it can access and revoke it the day someone leaves. - Siva Samy, ValGenesis, Inc.

Uncontrolled AI Access To Business Data

One of the biggest risks is giving AI access to business data without fully understanding what it can access or how that data will be used. Companies need clear rules around data access, permissions and how AI-generated outputs are used. The goal is to build those safeguards into the technology from the beginning rather than trying to address them later. - Steve Cangiano, CMiC

AI Agents As Insider Threats

AI agents act like humans, but they consume and move data far faster than any person could, often with more permissions than they need. Organizations need to govern them the way they govern insider risk: by understanding intent and behavior, not just access. In practice, that means connecting your AI security strategy to your data security strategy. Treat them as separate, and the gaps become the risk. - Sumit Dhawan, Proofpoint

AI-Generated Identity Fraud

Single-signal identity checks are obsolete. Fraudsters now use injection attacks and AI-generated media to bypass liveness checks, so a face or document that looks real proves nothing on its own. Verification must be continuous rather than a one-time onboarding checkbox, layering device and network signals, behavioral biometrics, and risk-based orchestration that pulls them together to build trust. - Kaarel Kotkas, Veriff

AI-Enabled Hiring Fraud

AI is turning hiring fraud into a real security threat. A fake candidate can now get through multiple stages of a hiring process, seem credible on paper and even ace interviews. If that person is hired, the company may hand an attacker legitimate access to internal systems, customer data, source code or financial information. Before giving candidates access to sensitive systems or data, companies need to verify that they really are who they say they are. - Gergo Vari, Lensa, Inc.

Sensitive Data Leaks Through Shadow AI

A widely underestimated risk is data leakage through shadow AI: employees quietly pasting sensitive customer, financial or IP data into unapproved tools whose retention, security and training practices IT cannot see. Bans can drive usage further underground. Organizations need better visibility to enforce responsible use and risk‑based controls that protect data without slowing innovation. - Neal Bradbury, Barracuda

AI Observability And Compliance Gaps

While the focus is more on AI-based cost savings or productivity, emphasis on observability and compliance needs equal attention; if overlooked, it will lead to regulatory and credibility issues, along with an auditability nightmare. These vital layers decide the distance between a proof of concept and successful production of AI agents. - Shammy Narayanan, Welldoc

Overreliance On AI-Generated Outputs

The biggest risk for me is not that AI will stop obeying humans but that humans will make a habit of trusting AI automatically. Although we are investing in better agentic AI defenses, we should also invest more in the internal architecture of the cyber professional, because the pressure will only increase, and without a zen-like mental clarity, the wrong choices could be made. - Carlo Tortora Brayda, Cyber Eagle Project Inc.

Inadequate AI Data Security

I don’t think enough leaders realize that AI security is fundamentally a data problem, not a model, agent or user one. Regardless of how AI is leveraged, it cannot operate safely unless it’s working with data that is trusted, accurate and high-quality. Teams can ensure their data meets these standards by implementing comprehensive, foundational data security posture management. - Thyaga Vasudevan, Skyhigh Security

Loss Of Granular Data Access Controls

Many product organizations underestimate the challenge of maintaining data access control as they scale AI. AI-augmented search, analytics and content synthesis offer enormous value, but preserving fine-grained access to sensitive IP is complicated if data is extracted into a data lake. Digital thread strategies need governed AI access to operational data and context to preserve access policy integrity. - Leon Lauritsen, Aras

Unmonitored ‘Synthetic Insiders’

One underestimated AI security risk is the rise of the “synthetic insider.” AI agents are given access to systems and permission to act for employees. They are no longer just tools but start to behave like insiders. Their actions should be continuously monitored against the role and task they were intended to perform. In the agentic era, leaders need to know whether an agent’s activity made sense. - Aviv Nahum, Above Security

AI Document Retention And Deletion Gaps

Every doc uploaded to AI is a doc outside your retention policy. Company docs end up all over the place, including staff laptops. Staff upload docs because 1. there is no system with secure doc storage or 2. outside tooling is faster. Provide a fast and secure place for content that LLMs can access. Second, ensure docs are fully deleted. Ask AI vendors what happens to derived artifacts, embeddings, caches and backups when a source document is deleted. - Aaron Rallo, Trovia

Unclear Accountability For Autonomous AI

One underestimated AI security risk is unclear accountability as AI moves from recommending actions to executing them. Organizations should define what AI can access, what it can act on autonomously, what requires human approval, and who owns the outcome. AI governance must address not only what a system can do but also who is accountable when it acts. - Jayasri Ranganathan, Trinity Solar Inc.

AI-Accelerated Attacks Against Static Defenses

AI is collapsing the cost and time required for attackers to experiment. They can automate reconnaissance, generate thousands of attack variations, and continuously adjust based on what gets through. Static rules and known-pattern detection cannot adapt at the same rate. Organizations need behavioral and unsupervised detection to surface novel patterns, paired with real-time decisioning so newly identified risk can immediately inform controls. - Yinglian Xie, DataVisor

AI-Accelerated Post-Breach Exploitation

AI enables attackers to analyze stolen source code and cloud stacks at machine speed, exposing new vulnerabilities on the fly. Believing an attack is contained just by revoking initial access is untenable; block one vector, and attackers find another within hours. Businesses must move faster than feels comfortable, apply same-day patching, and treat self-inflicted downtime as the safer option. - Ryan Ikeler, MOXFIVE
